blocks.text: Peter explains the Pentecost event by quoting Joel, but his wording is not simply reproduced without interpretation: he adapts the Greek form of the passage, including the phrase “in the last days.” The quotation therefore frames what the crowd sees and hears through Joel’s prophecy without requiring that every element of Joel’s oracle has been exhausted in this one event. Christian use of Joel here should also not erase its Jewish setting or continuing Jewish interpretation.

Peter’s speech also builds its case through David’s words. This reflects a wider New Testament pattern in which psalms are quoted and echoed in arguments about Jesus’ suffering, resurrection, enthronement, and mission. In Acts 2, the quotations are integral to Peter’s argument, not decorative additions to it.

The crowd is said to recognize the speakers’ words in their own native languages or dialects. Acts therefore portrays an intelligible multilingual event. Its precise relationship to other early Christian descriptions of speech remains debated, so this scene should not automatically be treated as identical to every later reference to tongues. Peter’s address is also a literary speech within an ancient narrative, rather than a stenographic transcript, even if it may preserve earlier tradition.

The shared life in verses 44–45 describes voluntary selling and distribution in response to need. Acts presents this as a community ideal in its summary of the believers’ life; it does not state an explicit universal legal code that abolishes all personal possession.

Acts includes several prominent scenes in which faith or repentance, baptism, prayer, laying on of hands, tongues, prophecy, and reception of the Spirit do not always appear in the same order or with every feature present. That wider pattern cautions against making Acts 2’s sequence a compulsory template, or treating the absence of one sign as proof that someone is excluded.

Acts survives in early papyri and major Greek codices, including P45, P53, P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae; these witnesses preserve different portions and textual profiles. Codex Bezae and related witnesses contain a notably distinctive form of Acts, often called the Western text, so individual differences need to be assessed case by case. More broadly, historical evaluation of Acts calls for examining particular claims alongside independent evidence rather than assigning the entire work a blanket judgment.
